maintopic: CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house that I have requested the Canadian wheat board to arrange a conference in Vancouver commencing on Monday next to explore ways and means of expanding the volume of grain which can be moved into and out of Pacific coast ports. The conference will be representative of the principal agencies concerned with the movement of grain from the prairies to the Pacific coast and the movement of this grain to terminal elevators and into ocean vessels.
Invitations have been extended to the following organizations:	Canadian Pacific
Railway, Canadian National Railways, Alberta wheat pool, United Grain Growers Limited, Saskatchewan wheat pool, Pacific group of elevators, Vancouver grain exchange, Vancouver merchants exchange, Vancouver chamber of shipping, shipping federation of British Columbia, trade union representatives, national harbours board, the port warden, the board of grain commissioners for Canada and the Canadian wheat board. It is my intention to attend the conference along with officers of my department.
I want to make the purpose of the conference clear. It is my hope that through the cooperation of the organizations and interests invited, ways and means can be worked out to increase the grain movement through Pacific coast ports. I am hopeful also that those who
attend the conference will join in suggestions relating to long-range developments. I think it is the desire of all concerned that the full potential of the west coast grain movement be realized and that the capacity of west coast ports to receive and load grain is keeping abreast with market opportunities, particularly in the Far East.
The construction of the St. Lawrence seaway and additional storage capacity planned by the national harbours board at Montreal, along with private building in the outer St. Lawrence, have added greatly to the efficiency and the capacity of the St. Lawrence route. A new berth is being constructed at Churchill which will speed up the loading of ocean vessels at that port.
Elevator companies operating at Fort William and Port Arthur have work under way there which will improve the loading of grain and, particularly, the loading of ocean tonnage which comes to the lakehead.
Some years ago additional storage capacity was built at Halifax, and the Atlantic maritime ports are having one of the busiest seasons on record. It is the desire of the government that grain handling facilities at all our ports be brought up to the standards required of them in these times.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will have heard the minister's statement with interest, and will support any steps the government may take to expedite and enlarge shipments of grain through Pacific ports, especially in view of recent reports from such ports that there have been delays in such shipments.

maintopic: CONFERENCE TO EXPEDITE MOVEMENT THROUGH PACIFIC COAST PORTS
speechtext:
We
welcome the statement which has just been made by the minister, Mr. Speaker. We certainly hope that as a result of the conference there will be not only a speed-up in loadings through the port of Vancouver, but there will be also a discussion of the question of installing new and additional facilities. It is many, many years since there have been any extensions to the port of Vancouver. As a matter of fact the facilities of the port are less now than they were as a result of a fire many years ago. The facilities lost then have never been replaced.
In view not only of the recent complaints concerning delay in shiploadings, but also in view of the statements made within the

Starred Questions
past month that Vancouver cannot expect to have new lines coming in until port facilities are expanded, we certainly welcome this announcement. We hope satisfactory conclusions can be arrived at and that speedy action will be taken to implement those conclusions.

maintopic: BANK OF CANADA SALES TO INVESTMENT ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for reasons of public policy which I think will be obvious to hon. members, it has never been the practice to disclose individual transactions of purchase or sale in relation to the securities investment account. Mr. Halliwell, a graduate in economics of the University of Saskatchewan, formerly an editorial writer and reporter with the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, reporter, agricultural writer and editorial writer with the Winnipeg Tribune and recently of the Toronto Telegram, is employed under contract by the Department of Agriculture as approved by treasury board and minute 574516 of January 23, 1961.

Since this observation is applicable to all wheat board operations, and since farmers are entitled to know what is being done by the board on their behalf, the professional

maintopic: CHURCHILL, MAN.    STATEMENT ON LOSS BY FIRE AT ROCKET BASE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CHURCHILL, MAN.    STATEMENT ON LOSS BY FIRE AT ROCKET BASE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Is the minister now in a position to advise the house as to the extent of the fire damage at the rocket launching site near Fort Churchill?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: CHURCHILL, MAN.    STATEMENT ON LOSS BY FIRE AT ROCKET BASE
speechtext:
I received notice of a question in this regard from the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) and I give the following answer.
The buildings seriously damaged in the rocket research facilities were the assembly area, including the garage portion and the test equipment area; the lunch room and the generator room adjacent to the assembly room. The fire travelled along the tunnel and involved the block house. There was minor damage to the launch tower itself owing to the activities of the firefighters.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The equipment destroyed included the technical stores test apparatus in the assembly area, two 60 KVA and two 50 KVA generators in the generator room, and the fire control equipment in the block house.
The buildings and equipment were entirely United States owned. There may have been some Canadian equipment in the lunch room or in the assembly area, and there may also have been some D.R.B. equipment in the block house, but this is not yet known.
A board of inquiry is being convened by the commander at Fort Churchill, with a Canadian officer as president and a United States officer as a member of the board.
The Canadian losses are relatively insignificant in comparison with the total loss, although it is impossible at this time to calculate the amount with any degree of certainty.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. Leon Balcer (Minisier of Transport).
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the inquiry by the hon. member for Assiniboia about a report regarding an increase in insurance rates for shipping using the St. Lawrence seaway, I understand that an increase is contemplated but is not solely related to the St. Lawrence seaway. It is for inland navigation as well as navigation on the great lakes.
I should emphasize that these rates are not under the control of the government but are set by the private companies which write the insurance in the light of shipping experience. The only thing we can do is to ensure that in so far as our governmental facilities are concerned we have done everything possible

to avoid the risk of accidents, and this we most certainly have done and will continue to do.
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises me that while there were 110 vessels involved in accidents within the seaway proper during the 1959 navigation season, there were only 41 vessels involved in accidents in the same area during the 1960 navigation season.

Mr. Speaker, with reference to the question asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia concerning a letter from the secretary-treasurer of the employees' local federation of the Canadian National Railways system in Edmonton and the two questions on the same matter by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, may I say that I duly received a copy of the letter and referred it to the management of the Canadian National Railways, who inform me there is not a nationwide lay-off scheduled to take place on March 17, nor is there any large scale lay-off in contemplation. I may say that the hon. member for Edmonton West has also spoken to me about this matter.
The management does point out, however, that the level of the working force of the railway will vary both upward and downward under the influence of seasonal requirements and traffic volume. There are some reductions, approximately 30, being made at various points throughout the mountain region because of lack of work.
With respect to the telegrams received by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, I made inquiries of the management and I am informed that five car helpers at Fort Frances are affected and three labourers at Rainy River.
Both hon. members made some reference to the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act, and I am assured by the management that the provisions of the act have been scrupulously observed.

I was just at the point of expressing my thanks to the standing committee on veterans affairs for the careful attention they gave to the bill when it was before that committee, and for bringing to our attention matters which require some adjustment.
Pension Act
We have reached the stage in this bill where we are close to concluding our deliberations. We had a lengthy debate as will be recalled at the resolution stage. The bill was up for second reading and was then referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs for a detailed study. It is now back before us for our consideration section by section. The bill appears to have met with general approval and I hope that the house will be able to deal with it expeditiously today. When we have third reading it will be sent to the other place for their consideration.
As I pointed out earlier in respect of this bill, we have attempted to bring up to date certain aspects of pension legislation that required attention. We have to a certain extent met suggestions that have been put before us by the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations. The main feature of the bill is to increase pension rates for disabled pensioners. This increase averages 20 per cent across the board and will bring the disabled pensioners' pensions more in line with what has always been intended with regard to pensions. These pensions are partial compensation for injuries suffered on the battlefields. It has been the intention of parliament over the years to have pensions correspond to average incomes in various categories in the country. From time to time the pensions have fallen below those averages. We are at this stage by this increase bringing them up to a position which I think is proving acceptable to our pensioners in Canada. I hope that the house will be able to approve this bill this afternoon-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are pleased that the minister accepted the amendments which will help to eliminate some of the problems that have existed. I wish, however, to point out the need for hon. members on all sides of the committee to give consideration to urging the government to reinstate the basis upon which the pension was initially granted.
Originally the disability pension was to be approximately equal to the lowest wage rate in the country, namely the wage commanded by the pick and shovel man. Gradually over the years we have lost sight of this ratio. When the various veterans organizations asked for an increase of 33J per cent they were not even asking that the ratio be reinstated to its original premise.
The national council of veterans associations point out how the relationship between the disability pension and the average wage in Canada has altered over the years to the disadvantage of the pensioners.
According to the national council which comprises such organizations as the Hong Kong veterans organization, the average wage rate in Canada in 1939 was $1,220. The basic pension at that time was $900 which represented 74 per cent of the average wage. In 1947 the average wage had increased to $1,800 and the basic pension to $1,128, a decrease in the ratio to 60 per cent. In 1951 the wage rate had increased to $2,480 and the basic pension to $1,500, the pension representing 60.5 per cent of the average wage. In 1957 the average wage had increased to

$3,520 and the basic pension to $1,800, a decrease in the ratio to 51 per cent. Hon. members in all parts of the committee should give consideration to urging the government to return the relationship between the basic pension and the average wage to a more equitable basis.
The government, of course, may increase pensions as it sees fit but I think consideration should be given to the proposition I have advanced especially in view of the fact that today we encourage young people to enlist in the armed services.
I was not present at the last meeting of the committee on veterans affairs but what occurred there tends to dispel the belief that no party politics are played with respect to veterans affairs. Various veterans organizations will read with some interest the discussions which took place in the committee. I was surprised at the extent to which politics entered those discussions. I was amazed that hon. members felt under an obligation to follow the instructions of the government instead of advancing their own ideas and making constructive recommendations. The practice of following the wish of the government in this and other committees should not be followed in the future. Particularly with respect to the committee on veterans affairs it is important that politics should not enter the discussion.
I did not participate in the previous debate with respect to this legislation because I wanted to see what would be the result of the deliberations of the standing committee. I am pleased that to a large extent the minister is ignoring the political implications that have arisen in respect of this bill and has suggested today that he will bring in amendments in keeping with the recommendations of the committee.

I am greatly interested in something that happened in this house a few weeks ago in relation to this bill, namely the discussion of the clauses required to make the provisions retroactive and the accusations which were made at that time together with the results of those accusations.
I hasten to say that in my remarks I certainly did not accuse either members or the chairman of the committee on veterans affairs of engaging in politics, but politics certainly entered into this matter and I should like to refer to the report of the committee on February 23. At that time there was before the committee a motion moved by two members of the opposition. Here is one of the statements that were made. I do not think we need refer to the hon. member who made it although that could be done if it were desired. The statement is as follows:
May I say this? As long as I have been associated with this committee on veterans affairs this is the first occasion on which political partisanship has come into play.
Then the statement goes on:
I shall be glad to make my statement without political bias. However, it is a fact that members of the government are placed in an awkward position.
Then, after some other statements by another member, the record continues:
I wish to say that I am not speaking against these payments being made retroactive. I am in favour of these increases being made to the veterans pensions. I have worked for them consistently for many months, and I believe that the most expeditious way in having them brought in at the earliest moment is for this committee to support the government in the method which they have chosen to bring in these increases, thereby taking no chances for a further delay in the matter. Our best course is to follow along the lines which have been set by the government.
Another hon. member goes on to say:
We are torn, as it were, between two choices, like a father with two sons. If a recommendation has been made by the cabinet, or by the minister, and apparently it has been, I submit that the government members have no other alternative than to support our government. But on the other hand, we are all veterans: we know how much this means to them, I think that we are being put on the spot.
I suggest that there were political overtones in this statement. In my remarks I did not enter upon a discussion of what those political overtones were. If you still think I am being unfair, Mr. Chairman, I will quote from other sections in the report statements which indicate that many of the members have not yet grown up to the stage where they are able to face their responsibility and make recommendations on the basis of their own opinions. Instead, it is clear they are inclined to prejudge what the government or the cabinet or the minister will do.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
As I said before, I am pleased with the statement which the minister has now made. It is a statement which shows that some members of the committee were prejudging the minister incorrectly, because it appears that the hon. gentleman himself is probably going to make the recommendations as to which the members of the committee should have taken a stand on their own initiative instead of hedging, perhaps in belief that to do otherwise would run counter to their membership in a political party.
I would only point out that these basic requests have been made by organizations to which many of us belong and which most of us support. I have been a member of the Canadian Legion for many years and, speaking for myself, I may say I am one of those who fall into the category mentioned by the last speaker. If this increase becomes effective I will receive an increase in my pension, though it will not be enough to make any difference one way or another. Incidentally, that fact is not to be taken as a reason why I was not at that meeting or as a reason why I would have refused to vote for it.
This is my contention. We should bear in mind the fact that we have an obligation to the veterans to bring their pensions in line with the average wage in the country which they would be entitled to receive if they were in a physical condition enabling them to perform work in that line. Veterans' pensions should bear a fair and just relationship to the average wage in the country. I think we should bear that fact in mind. I am not criticizing anybody and I have not mentioned anybody.
I think we should bear in mind the fact that we should deal with veterans affairs in a non-political way, and hope this will always be the case. The political party to which we belong should not be taken into consideration. We should have consideration only for the larger organization to which we belong, namely the veterans organizations, and the veterans' preference and veterans' status that all members of the committee have attained because of the service they have given to their country should be kept in mind.

On clause 8, Mr. Chairman, we have an amendment to suggest; it is rather lengthy and somewhat complicated. In substance, what it amounts to is this. The amendment will do two things. It will increase the maximum payable from $480 per year to $576 per year, and it will increase the ceiling from $576 per year to $1,296 per year to the dependent parent where the pensioner has died leaving a pensionable child but there is no widow entitled to the pension.
Section 38, subsection 2 of the Pension Act now reads that the pension to the dependent parent cannot exceed the amount stipulated in the section so long as there is either a child or a widow, either or both of whom are entitled to pension. Under the new legislation the child's pension will not be considered in deciding to pension the dependent parent.
This change adds to the financial obligation of the government, I think, only about $75,000 in a grand total of approximately $30 million that we have been considering, but it will count in part of the resolution that we had to use to precede the study of the bill in committee of the whole house.

When I spoke on this subject previously I mentioned what we could achieve here and compared that with what had been done in the United States in connection with the Tennessee valley authority project. This project was conceived primarily to deal with wasteland in the Tennessee valley but had the related objectives of community development, soil and water conservation and the provision of recreational facilities. It is my hope that when this legislation is introduced its provisions will be wide enough to permit that type of regional planning, particularly with regard to agriculture. I must, of course, relate it to agriculture. This country needs that type of development in many of the areas of what I might call the perimeter of the development. Agriculture in these areas must become more diversified and more sophisticated. We do not want to see the elimination of agriculture or those farmers brought into the cities who are on what we might call the borderline of making a livelihood and who depend on the type of rural redevelopment in that particular region.
My belief is that this scheme could well be applied on the basis of regional and river-basin area development. I refer, of course, to my own district, namely the Peace river area. May I say in passing, sir, that just recently the President of the United States sent to congress a message in the course of which he underlined the fact that the proper maximum development of the national resources, including agriculture, in his country could well be increased by means of proceeding along regional lines. I believe in yesterday's Toronto Globe and Mail I noticed a news item dealing with the report made by a professor A. K. Cairncross of the University of Glasgow who had made an inspection of the Atlantic area and reported to the premiers of those areas. Professor Cairncross stated that, in his opinion, this country had reached a stage where it must seriously consider regional planning.
A great many things are included in that matter, Mr. Chairman, and I believe they fit within the four corners of this resolution. I refer to soil and water conservation, reforestation, the provision of recreational areas, community development, the development of electric power, and so on. In that connection, may I say that I was very greatly interested in reading not long ago that something along this line had been done in Manitoba, not on the basis of regional planning but on the basis of community planning. This was not a case of large sums of money being given to the community by senior governments. The people living in these agricultural communities and in the market towns which

serve them had been helped to help themselves. These people had laid the groundwork, done the planning and persuaded secondary industries to come into the area in order to give them a more diversified way of life. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is what we might well do under the terms of this particular resolution and the bill which will follow it.
There is one further feature in connection with regional planning and regional development as applied to agriculture areas. We find that governments now must accumulate unto themselves a large repository of power in order to meet the centralization of industry, the growth and centralization of unions and so on. I believe we all agree that is necessary, but regional planning along the lines I suggest would permit a decentralization of power, a decentralization of the administrative authority. I want to relate that matter particularly to the development of the Tennessee valley district.
There was obtained the consent of seven states and the federal government to yield to some extent a portion of their authority, and to vest that authority in a T.V.A. commission. This commission, vested with this authority from the states and the federal government, was able to provide a type of autonomous authority which was of great benefit to the district concerned. It would be good under legislation of this kind to vest authority in a local autonomy in order to allow the carrying into effect of the plans of a regional authority such as the one I have mentioned, and to allow it to exercise that authority without being forced to return to Ottawa, Edmonton, Victoria or the other provincial capitals.
When I refer to the procedural aspect of this resolution I feel that it offers a fair opportunity for advancement. We are in the stage of our national development in which we are ripe for the benefits which will flow from this resolution. I have related this resolution to my own district, namely the Peace River country, an area which up to the present time has been almost exclusively restricted to agriculture. At this time we are now coming to the stage of secondary industry, with pulp mills, logging, timber mills, the development of natural gas and petroleum resources, and many other improvements in our way of life and the way in which our people are able to earn a living. The difficulty we have faced in the past has been the necessity of going to Victoria, Edmonton and Ottawa for authority, and most of the development which I have described has been seriously hampered and hindered by this type of divided authority.

As I said before, I am realist enough to believe that we will never change the situation so far as the provincial authorities are concerned, so far as the boundaries are concerned; but, through the medium of the agencies which are envisaged by this resolution, I am confident that we can make up much of the ground we have lost. For this reason I am pleased to give my strong support to this resolution. I hope that it will meet with the approval of all members.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution which the committee of the whole is now discussing relates to the development and rehabilitation of agricultural areas.
When the resolution was introduced on January 25 last, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) stated that 21 per cent of the Canadian farms yield less than $1,200 a year to their operators. As far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned, the picture is much darker still than for the country as a whole. These are, by provinces, the figures quoted by the minister:

Today, I should like to deal with that problem more particularly as it relates to the province of New Brunswick.
Mr. Chairman, in order to avoid hasty conclusions on the face of those statistics, it is necessary that the scope of the question be enlarged. Indeed, I believe that the explanations given by the minister until now are much too succinct and do not reflect the issue from all its angles.
The statistics given by the minister are quoted from the 1956 census.
Now, this was the definition of a farm in connection with that census:
Any agricultural unit was considered a farm:
(a)	When the production value was $250 a year; and
(b)	when the acreage was three acres or more, without considering the production value.
Again according to the 1956 census, 24.4 per cent of farms in the province of New Brunswick contained from 1 to 50 acres, and 33.5 per cent from 51 to 100 acres of land.
In the light of those statistics, it is obvious that there is a close connection between income and acreage, and it would seem that if such a large proportion of farms in New Brunswick yield such an insignificant yearly income, the cause would have to be found in their size as well as in the quality of the soil. Yet, I am afraid that the Minister of Agriculture when introducing his resolution on January 25 last, left quite a different impression, namely that the low income from marginal or submarginal land was more particularly due to poor soil. That is an error which should be avoided when planning for the rehabilitation of some submarginal agricultural areas. That is why the first essential step when considering the problem would, to my mind, be a detailed classification of soils, in order to find out which are unsuitable for general farming. While it is important to turn to alternative uses any land which is unsuitable for general farming, all land which could produce food economically should be kept in production in New Brunswick.
When introducing his motion, the minister pointed out that agricultural over-production in our country should be taken into account. I must say that such conditions do not exist in New Brunswick, because, except for potatoes, we have to import from 50 to 75 per cent of all agricultural products we consume. The figures are 10 per cent for butter, 80 per cent

Marginal Lands
for cheese, 60 per cent for pork, 50 per cent for beef, 50 per cent for fowl, 35 per cent for eggs and 75 per cent for vegetables.
Need I say more to show that what is needed in New Brunswick is not a program to reduce agricultural production but rather a program to increase it?
On the occasion of a day of economic studies organized in Moncton by the extension department of St. Joseph's University, in December last, Mr. Camille Chiasson, an agronomist employed by the New Brunswick department of agriculture, dealt quite competently with the agricultural situation in the province. His remarks covered four aspects of the problem. These four points, to which I subscribe, are as follows:
1.	A regional development program. This implies a detailed survey of all resources of an area and requires the co-operation of all elements of the population: chambers of commerce, educators, clergymen, businessmen, professional associations, co-operatives, etc. To those who would claim that this problem is the sole concern of farmers and that they alone are responsible for a solution, I would recall the words of President Eisenhower who said that the minimum farm income of any area is not entirely an agricultural problem, but that it is related to the whole economy and that it can be settled only by the development of all the resources of the area.
The results of such a survey-they will necessarily vary from one area to another- will allow the guiding of agriculture in such or such direction: improving of farming or breeding methods; introduction of new crops and new marketing facilities; establishment of small industries, etc.
2.	The farmer will have to change or at least modernize his ideas. Those who work in our rural areas cannot help notice that the few farmers who succeed are those who have kept pace with conditions and brought in some changes such as an increase of their acreage and their stock, mechanization, specialization, etc. But they are a minority and it is surprising to see the great number of those who are still trying to earn their living on the few acres and the number of livestock which their grandfathers had.
This modernization is no less important in woodlot development. When one thinks of how much waste there is in the exploitation of our forest resources, one is surprised to see there are still some left.

In certain cases, it would be advisable to give back to the forest, marginal or poor lands that should never have been cleared.
3.	Where it is impossible to increase farm acreage, it would probably be possible to turn to special productions such as:
(a)	sheep, hog or poultry farming;
(b)	small fruit or vegetable farming;
(c)	blueberries;
(d)	Christmas trees.
4.	Production and marketing co-operatives. It seems a waste of time to insist on that point, but unfortunately there are too many farmers who are not convinced that there lies their only hope. One should look at what happened in the case of the specialized producers near the larger centers. In spite of the importance of their operations, they have been forced to unite in order to survive. There is no other means to prevent vertical integration.
I should like to point out now that the school would have a great contribution to make to an agricultural development project. Such was the argument of Hon. Adrien Levesque, minister of agriculture in the province of New Brunswick, presented in October last before a group of farmers meeting in Moncton. As a matter of fact, we may wonder to what degree the rural school as it is has delayed agricultural progress.
The fact is that our school system does not predispose the child to love the land and farming. Rather, it prepares our rural youth for life in the cities, not in the country. Not that the rural school should be raised to the level of an agricultural school, but it would only be normal, it seems to me, that without neglecting the teaching of basic subjects it should promote the development of a rural spirit and the knowledge of basic elements; of agriculture, which is totally defective in the present system.
One must say, in all fairness to certain areas of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, that certain traditions contribute to underline the agricultural importance of those areas. In those two provinces where potatoes are grown on a large scale, school opens two weeks earlier, that is around mid-August, but they are closed for a corresponding period during harvesting.
Such practice allows school boys to help the industry of the area at the time when labour is more in demand. I must say that where that practice prevails, agriculture is generally more prosperous than elsewhere. Would it be because, among other things,.

young people have been taught the importance of the industry which is the foundation of the regional economy?
In view of its relation to the matter we are now discussing in this house, I should like to quote part of an editorial published in L'Evangeline of October 26, 1960: Agriculture is now at the crossroads. Is society directing it towards an impersonal form of farming, whereby the land, having become the property of limited companies, will be scientifically developed by employees who have nothing to say on the management of the company, employees who most likely will be organized, and who will get a weekly salary like their counterparts in industry?
Must we accept the disappearance of farmers' traditional families, tilling the soil, breeding animals, with the help of their sons who thus prepare themselves to take over?
Agriculture must be reorganized in such a way as to allow farmers to enjoy a better way of life, in keeping with their status as land owners. When farmers once again occupy in society the first rank place which is theirs, it will then be easy to promote agricultural pride.
The day is gone when farmers' sons, anxious to operate a farm with success, could quit school when they were 14 years old. Today, farmers are facing technical problems requiring higher education, wide technical knowledge, and great competence.
The rural school should promote love of the farm through a greater awareness and better appreciation and show the way to prosperous farming through respect for everybody's rights and co-operation of each individual for the common welfare.
Mr. Chairman, it has been proved by now that agriculture must keep abreast of the times. Modern agriculture cannot perpetuate customs and routines passed on from father to son. The farmer has to apply new methods, increase his efficiency, and reduce his costs. Moreover, rational farming requires general regional planning involving the co-operation of all farmers in a spirit free from selfishness, pettiness and envy.
Mr. Chairman, those are the many problems which we have to face in respect of all proposed rural projects, and let us hope that the one we have before us will be the answer to the tremendous responsibilities we have to shoulder. In formulating the terms of this bill, and later on, in seeing to it that they are carried out, the government will have to seek the co-operation of all people of goodwill at all levels of our society. The aim is well worth the effort. The government should also consider the wise recommendations made by the Senate committee with regard to this matter.
I want to conclude my remarks by quoting some of the major recommendations of that committee, which might serve as a guide to everyone concerned. I quote:
Whereas there is a need of elimination of problem areas in Canada where farm businesses are
Marginal Lands
small, productivity low, and incomes inadequate for family requirements: The committee recommends,
(1)	(a) That further research be undertaken to define more clearly the nature of the problem in low income areas and to pinpoint their location.
(b) That a federal-provincial rural development program be instituted to deal with areas of greatest need.
(2)	That in implementing such a program the provincial governments participate on a co-operative basis; such co-operation to include the principle that both provincial and local authorities assume major responsibility for the identification of problems and needs of local areas and the initiation, planning and development of appropriate action programs.
(3)	That the federal and provincial governments co-operate in assisting any such program with financial and technical assistance, said financial assistance to be provided through a cost sharing agreement.
(4)	That the federal and provincial governments provide for a larger farm-management service and expansion of educational facilities with particular emphasis on leadership to ensure a prompt dissemination of the research results to those farmers who will be most benefited therefrom.
This program is comprehensive and will require a great outlay of funds. Nothing less, however, could provide an answer to the basic problem of our agriculture. It is the future of the family farm and of the whole farming community that is at stake.

speechtext:
I should like first of all to congratulate those hon. members who have already taken part in the discussion of this important resolution and I am certainly not excepting, but including, the last speaker who I think made a marvellous contribution to this debate.
This is, I think, one of the most important resolutions to come before us in this present session and I am happy to see the way in which this subject is being approached by members on all sides. The resolution itself is comprehensive and to my mind it is one of the most important to come before parliament since I have been a member. Actually it is in keeping with other progressive legislation introduced by the government this session. I am going to say this. I have been a member of the house for 17 years and I do not recall any other session during which so much progressive legislation has been introduced and passed in such a short period of time.
On reading the resolution one must conclude that it allows a great deal of freewheeling in discussion. There are two aspects of it to which I should like to address myself. You will have noticed, of course, Mr. Chairman, that one aspect of the motion deals with

Marginal Lands
the water resources of Canada and I should like, of course, to deal with that aspect in particular. There are, in fact, so many facets to it, that a member is not really given the opportunity to deal with all of them. I therefore intend to confine myself largely to the subject of the water supply. Then, if I have time in which to do so, I shall deal with the situation in Holland and Denmark with respect to farming, because conditions there are relatively the same as they are in Ontario.
Water pollution is, in itself, a broad subject but certainly it is going to be one of the major problems facing us. It is, I repeat, a problem, and its ultimate solution will be difficult. However, I am happy to note that this fact is being increasingly realized; and as a result of the work which will be done in consequence of the resolution being passed, I think a great deal will be accomplished. Serious attention must be paid to the water problem we face in this country. I say it is an extremely serious problem. I dealt with one aspect of it in an earlier speech and I hope to say more along the same lines today. I must say that the resolution is timely. As we all know, land use has been a matter for concern to the province of Ontario, and the government of that province has made extensive studies through the conservation council of Ontario and other agencies.
In this great era of change, with an accelerating tempo in almost every facet of our daily lives, the present so soon becomes the past that what we now do, and how we do it, must be equated with a critical eye to the future. This is not easy to do and yet so much depends on how well we do it.
The onrush of technological progress bears with it the hope for the future and, at the same time, a deep concern for the potential dangers it holds. While we exploit the one, we need to take extreme care to understand and to minimize the other. We must be sure that our concepts and our practices are attuned to the times and will keep the scales tilted in favour of man, his health and his well-being. From the monthly letter of the Royal Bank of Canada, Vol. 41, No. 4, entitled, "The Relationship of Man and Nature," I should like to quote as follows:
To subdue nature, to bend its forces to our will, has been the acknowledged purpose of mankind since human life began, but the time has come for a revision of our conception of the benefits and responsibilities of holding dominion over all other created things. A new spirit is abroad as scientists and laymen realize that man and the rest of nature are united and individible.
At a time when great elemental forces are clamouring at the bars of our civilization, we need to discard our ideas of 'attacking' the forest, 'bringing under subjection' the mighty rivers, 'con-
quering' the mountains and 'subduing' the prairie. Instead, we need to make the most of all nature as an ally.
Somehow or other the basis of any conservation program must be tied to the continuing economic welfare of the nation regardless of the individual. The use of our soil and water, forest and streams, must eventually be restricted to those who respect and cherish this franchise. The establishment of this principle must be developed and accepted as part of our national attitude just as other rules of conduct are written into our way of life. They protect the individual as they protect the nation. This is very much the case with regard to food and water. Even the presence of water has not always assured man of his food. Abundance often breeds laziness, and the subsequent neglect of water resources can bring stagnation to man and his food production.
I have had the pleasure of attending in this country and in the United States, many meetings on conservation, particularly concerning water pollution which knows no boundaries. Here is a problem area in which we need to break down the barriers of provincialism, the prejudices of proprietary interest, and the varieties of narrow, hereditary points of view, too commonly shared by so many of us. We all recognize that our advancing society needs more water for domestic use and much more water to produce the things we eat, wear and use. To provide adequate water in usable form, when and where needed, and to do this within a reasonable cost, is essential to our way of life.
It is an interesting commentary in this technological era that the availability of adequate water, the world's most plentiful substance, remains an essential key to man's progress. In this country and on this continent our water resources, their use and misuse, are rapidly becoming a prime critically urgent national problem. Beyond satisfying thirst, there is no single water problem but rather a multiplicity of complex problems, issues and questions spanning the technical, political and social fields. In composite these constitute the ingredients that make up public water policy and, in turn, such policy goes to the very heart of our economy.
What we do, for instance, in making available sufficient water determines in a major way the location and prosperity of industry and its supporting populations. For most industries the availability of water is more important even than is the proximity to raw materials or to markets; and the manner in which this water is used affects agriculture, wild life, recreational facilities and the like.

Consideration must be given to the problem so that the ideal habitat of water fowl and wild life will be protected. I am referring to marshes. When we talk about comparative use we must consider the simple mathematics of space.
Another fundamental consideration is the control of water resources. The manner in which this matter is ultimately resolved draws the pattern of land use of great areas of our continent. Among the things to be considered are the impact of water shortages, the complexities of interregional conflicts, the urgency for expanding beneficial uses. All of these demand not necessarily control but attention and action and some degree of co-ordination.
In the North American countries and, of course, elsewhere each of us has a personal and a proprietary interest in how this is done and even more specifically, where and how the authority for doing it is located and administered. To put the water problem in perspective we must first focus on man, his patterns of behaviour and his new-found upsurging technology. May I say this by way of illustration, and this is very important. The great lakes and their connecting rivers are the natural boundary between the United States and Canada for some 1,100 miles, from Duluth to Kingston. The United States population now approaches 180 million, being up 40 per cent in two decades. The metropolitan growth trend will continue. Within two decades, three quarters of this wall to wall population will live in metropolitan centres. We are seeing the development of gigantic metropolitan complexes extending hundreds of miles along superhighways and major waterways. This development also applies to Canada but to a lesser extent. Technological growth is even more fantastic. This statement holds when viewed by any yardstick you might choose, such as gross national product, raw materials, energy requirements, transportation or communications.
In addition to the oil and gas drilling menace to the great lakes, we must realize that the chemical industry and the petrochemical industry are two segments of our economy which are showing phenomenal growth. Synthetic chemicals, plastics, detergents, pesticides, solvents and the like are skyrocketing, not only in quantities but also in diversity. Literally hundreds of new chemicals come into production and use each year. To illustrate, may I point out that these facts, in the field of plastics in the United States in 1940, production was 150 million pounds. Last year it was well over 5 billion pounds. Synthetic detergents increased in 20 years from 15 million pounds to 1.3 billion
Marginal Lands
pounds. For the same period production of synthetic pesticides and other agricultural chemicals increased from 8 million to 540 million pounds. I cite these particular examples because of their impact as potential pollutants on our water resources, and these will have a great effect on the waters of the great lakes. Our production, Mr. Chairman, as you know, is in proportion to the population of the United States.
In the backwash of these tidal waves are growing needs for usable water and greater competition. These factors will tax to the limit our fresh water resources. It is therefore no wonder that, as a resident on lake Huron and as chairman of the Canadian-American committee on water pollution, I am greatly concerned about oil and gas drilling in the great lakes. We all know that the leases are granted by the provincial government of Ontario. Any pollution from this source concerns several of our departments of government, including external affairs, fisheries, public works, transport, national health and welfare, agriculture and northern affairs and national resources; yet we find ourselves handicapped because we cannot take action unless there is extensive pollution.
I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to pay tribute to the international joint commission which has made great strides in co-operation with the Ontario government and the federal government of the United States in studying the problem and recommending measures to abate the pollution.
A few moments ago I gave an illustration with regard to a run-away oil well not too far from the shores of lake Huron, in Michigan, from which, before it was capped, 100,000 barrels of oil were released. It seems unfortunate that we are obliged to wait for something like this to happen before we can do anything. Yet the provincial government continues to grant leases for oil exploration, which might more properly be termed oil exploitation in many cases, in lake Erie where companies operating for 30 years have never paid a dividend.
Under this resolution I must bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the presence of oil in our water in the great lakes would do much to crucify our tourist industry, our bird life and our fishing, and it would be a menace to health since we in western Ontario are no doubt going to have to depend on our water supply from lake Huron, and this factor is certainly going to affect our agricultural production. I have said

Marginal Lands
before that the area from Toronto to Windsor will be depending on water from Georgian bay and lake Huron before 10 or 15 years have passed.
The national anarchy in water pollution policy and control programs must be ended. It is time for the province of Ontario and the federal government to get together and see the problems and work together to correct them. This must, of course, be done in co-operation with the United States. Today the people are pollution conscious and want action. The federal government can do something about pollution from the ships which are using the great lakes, and the Ontario government can reconsider its policy of contributing to pollution in the great lakes by issuing licences to drill on property they have already leased to these exploration or exploitation companies. We find one agency of the provincial government insisting on sewage treatment plants, and the plants we have in the east and have maintained previously are not good enough; and we find another agency of government granting leases for oil and gas drilling to foul the waters of our great lakes system. Let us stop fouling our own most important natural resource.
While I am on this subject and since I have spoken on this matter previously in the house, I should like to say that we have been complaining about this objectionable oil and gas drilling in the great lakes by those companies which maintain, as they have maintained over the years, that there is no danger of spillage with all their modern technology and new equipment. A moment ago I gave an illustration of the spillage of 100,000 barrels of oil from a well before it was capped. What would have happened had the oil well been in a lake?
I am happy to have heard not long ago from the front benches of this government that some consideration is being given by the federal government of the United States and our federal government to a problem which has faced our two countries for many years, namely the habit of vessels on the great lakes using the great lakes to dump their used oil and sewage. The conclusion of the study should not be too long delayed. In fact, it has been delayed for 50 years, a period which is too long. The quicker this problem is solved the better; and it can be solved because we in this country and the people of the United States want that body of fresh water kept fresh in spite of any government action or inaction.
I am now going to refer to something that was brought to the government's attention last fall. The government must take heed of the protests from the east coast of our country against the practice of the atomic energy

commission of the United States in dumping radioactive wastes some few miles off the coast; I do not know how many miles it is. However, I think one of the hon. members from New Brunswick or Nova Scotia raised this question last fall.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that this dumping of radioactive waste offers a new and potentially dangerous pollutant of the nation's water courses. The most serious potential danger to our long range health as far as water pollution is concerned will arise when the radioactive waste dumped at sea by the atomic energy commission starts spreading through the oceans. "Out of sight, out of mind" is not a very satisfactory way in which to handle this problem.
So far, since 1951 the atomic energy commission of the United States has dumped at sea 23,000 steel and concrete barrels filled with radioactive waste, and an A.E.C. spokesman has conceded that these barrels break up in ten years or less. Surely there are other places in the United States, such as rock caves, and so on, where this waste can be dumped until perhaps some years hence there can be a safe disposal system.
I think it is a crime that this practice has been allowed to continue and I am going to suggest to the government that the time for action is now. If these barrels, as has been indicated, will contain this radioactive waste for a period of only ten years or less, this material is then free to flow in the oceans. It is true that the oceans are big but it is also true that there must be plenty of space in the United States, in caverns or other places, where they can store this radioactive waste until the scientists of their country or some other country can determine a safe method of disposal. This nation should not stand idly by and let the United States atomic energy commission dump their continually increasing amount of radioactive waste into the Atlantic ocean or any other ocean.
Previously during this session of parliament I spoke about our sand beaches on the great lakes and referred to their pollution. Sand beaches are important in this or any other country because they afford to hundreds of thousands of youngsters and their parents the opportunity to use these beaches for recreation. Let us not deny them that opportunity in this country.
We in Ontario and people in most parts of Canada are blessed with a great deal of shoreline on the great lakes and on inland lakes and rivers but our population at the moment is only 18 million people or a little better. Consider the situation in the United States. At the moment around metropolitan areas such as Milwaukee, Chicago, Cleveland and

Detroit, none of which is very far from the capital of Canada, existing public ownership on the great lakes provides for only one quarter inch of frontage per person living within 50 miles of the shore. There is not a beach on the great lakes that does not show evidence of oil. For thousands of miles on our side of the great lakes every sand beach and every other kind of beach, according to samples taken last year, showed evidence of used oil. It is no wonder that the minister of energy resources in Ontario is much concerned about the practice of ships dumping their used oil into our great lakes system.
I share with him that view and, as I said a moment ago, I hope that our government in conjunction with the United States government will see that this practice is stopped. As I said, this situation is caused by ships using the great lakes. In co-operation with the government of the United States our government can require ships using the great lakes to have on board containers into which their sewage, garbage and old oil can be dumped for proper disposal at some municipal sewage treatment plant. The people of Ontario have put up with this situation for long enough and the time for action is now. I said before and I say again that where people become pollution conscious, as the people of my constituency in southwestern Ontario have become-and I am sure the same should be true of many more areas in Ontario at least-they are more conscious of pollution than they are of taxes.
When I spoke previously I said that I should like to deal with the application of science to agriculture as found in Denmark and Holland. These two countries are today practising scientific farming more effectively than is any other country in the world. While it is true that the land both in Denmark and Holland is relatively flat and that in many sections the soil is particularly good, there are other areas where the soil is far from satisfactory, so that the average high yield per acre recorded for these two countries cannot be credited to soil or climate.
Holland and Denmark have a high agricultural productivity. Holland has a population of approximately 10 million and Denmark 5 million compared with Ontario's population of approximately 5 million. The climate in both European countries is about the same as that in central and southwestern Ontario so that farming conditions should be somewhat similar in the three countries. For many years I have wondered why the farmers in Ontario did not make the same effective use of new discoveries as industry was making on the North American continent. A study of agricultural conditions in Holland
Marginal Lands
and Denmark shows that farming does not need to lag behind industry as these two countries are adapting the same approach in agriculture that big industry has found so effective. The three main factors that have contributed to the extraordinary accomplishments of Holland and Denmark are:
(1) agricultural education, so effective and extensive that it reaches into every farm home in the country; (2) a large and effective advisory service, adequately supported by research institutes, experimental farms, pilot farms and demonstration fields; (3) an agricultural federation operated by farmers that gives a large measure of support and to an increasing degree guides the research and experimental policy of the two countries.
While the results accomplished are similar in Holland and Denmark, the methods they employ are quite different. In Holland the educational system is similar to that practised in Canada only it is far more intensive, starting with the young farmers and continuing through the training of agricultural scientists. In Denmark the training of the agricultural scientists is the responsibility of the state, but the training of the farm youth, either at boarding schools, folk high schools or agricultural high schools, is the responsibility of the communities these schools serve. While the state makes some contributions to the operation of the 28 agricultural colleges that train some 2,500 pupils, the direction and operation are the responsibility of local boards. In addition, night classes during the winter are attended by some 90,000 pupils.
In both Holland and Denmark practical farm experience is considered to be most important and those wishing to enter agricultural schools or to hold any post of importance must have several years' training on a good farm. As seen from the foregoing, agricultural education is held in high esteem in the two European countries.
In Holland the professors at Wagingen are responsible for teaching and the carrying on of independent research. Research institutes, of which there are about 22, are financed by the state but the direction is by a board of directors composed of farmers, college professors, research officials and government representatives.
The advisory services, which have nothing to do with the research institutes, have their own experimental units in different parts of the country. It is in these units that the more practical aspects of research are developed. In addition, many thousands of farm and field experiments are carried on by the farmers under the direction of the agricultural advisers. All senior agricultural advisers are university graduates. The assistants, of whom

Marginal Lands
there are a great many, are graduates of agricultural schools who in addition have had many years of practical training in the research institutes, advisory service units and experimental farms. Because the advisory services have their own experimental units, those wishing to sell farmers new fertilizer, spray material or farm equipment find it advantageous to obtain first of all the approval of the agricultural adviser before approaching the farmers, though this procedure is not obligatory. In addition to the foregoing, the farmers federation is responsible for all quality control whether seed, fruit, flowers or dairy products. In fact, the federation operates many control laboratories. In addition, they operate several soil testing laboratories and finance and operate the farm economic institute at The Hague which employs over 200 people.
The federation is yearly increasing its contribution to the research program of the country. The farmers sit on all research institutes and advisory service boards, and take a direct interest in quality control, economic and research programs. In Holland, many farmers may see a film depicting an experiment which includes the work evaluation of the farmers, the planting and harvesting of crops, the care of cattle and improved living conditions for the people, all of which can be accomplished by the application of science to rural life.
In Denmark agricultural activities are handled in a unique manner. With the exception of the agricultural college and the research farms, practically every activity is controlled and directed by the farmers federation, not by the state. In the case of the college and the research farms, the farmers make up the majority of the boards of each institute. Agricultural advisers, of which there are over 600 or one to every three or four hundred farms-and by the way, may I say that there are eight to ten times as many in Denmark as there are in Canada -are appointed either by the federation or local farmers' associations. The government contributes only about 25 per cent to the operating cost of these services. There are innumerable plant and animal breeding stations throughout the country and farm and field experiments are numbered in the thousands, practically all operated by farmers under the direct supervision of the agricultural advisers. In contrast to Holland, the Danes train farmers to keep first-class books, so that with a relatively small staff of economists they are able to obtain comprehensive figures on yields and quality of products throughout the country. Neither Holland nor Denmark operate with subsidies, their philosophy being that good cultural practice is better than

state support. In either country, there is no arbitrary control of the farmers but through demonstrations and persuasion they are encouraged to adopt new scientific methods of farming.
In order to illustrate what extensive scientific application has accomplished in Holland and Denmark, may I make the following few observations.
In so far as Holland is concerned, during the last four years there has been a very marked increase in the amount of grass cut for drying, pressing and silaging. A breed of sheep has been developed that averages 1.88 lambs a year. Strains of fruit trees are under government control. Nurseries receive their scions from experimental stations. Practically all new orchards of apples and pears are dwarf trees, as it is claimed that the early bearing makes it more economical than planting normal size trees.
In so far as Denmark is concerned, over 75 per cent of all cows are bred by artificial insemination. There are 22 progeny testing stations where the quantity and quality of milk produced from heifers is determined in order to build up the average milk production. The same type of progeny control is practised with swine and other livestock, so that even though the present average production is at a high level, it is anticipated that this will still increase due to the new methods of improving livestock.
