subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. As one of the older members of the house, I should like to pay tribute to the minister for introducing at this time such an important resolution which will have such an effect on our economy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture upon the introduction of this resolution and this new approach to agriculture in Canada. I greatly appreciate being given the chance of expressing my views on certain phases of it. I presume this resolution arose partly as a result of the review of the rural development program in the United States which was undertaken at the request of the Senate special committee on land use in Canada. I am well acquainted with the four members of the Department of Agriculture who made this investigation. The senior member was Dr. Booth, an expert in agriculture economics.
I wanted to make a few remarks somewhat along the same lines as those made by the hon. member for Peace River, especially as they related to the stand of the federation

of agriculture on this subject. I received the federation brief yesterday and I read through it rather quickly. I should like to quote from that part of the brief dealing with land and water use and rural development. It reads:
Broad enabling legislation is being introduced to parliament by the Minister of Agriculture at this session. We welcome this legislation, as you know, since it promises to meet major demands of Canadian Federation of Agriculture policy and important needs of farmers.
As a member of the agriculture institute for Canada, I am certain that the resolution will receive the support of this group of scientific agriculturalists. This institute has a membership of 3,065 at the moment. One prominent member of the institute in my province recently wrote to me, and I should like to read a part of his letter:
As an agrologist, I am very much inclined to the opinion that the government is to be commended for developing leadership in respect to land use, especially as it pertains to further increase of forest resources. In the long term, the proposal to utilize lands that are submarginal agriculturally for forest is very worth while. I understand that world requirements for pulp alone are going to overtax present softwood stands within a surprisingly few years. In my opinion, the forest resource is actually an agricultural resource and its further development is absolutely dependent on the application of agricultural techniques.
Recognizing the food surplus situation in respect to North America and the fact that the European mainland anticipates substantial agricultural surpluses within five years, I am satisfied that there is every justification for developing where practicable submarginal lands for the production of softwood for pulp and other timber requirements. In the long term, forestry is an excellent provider of employment. However, I am in no position to say how successful a planning program would be in providing employment over the next 30-50 years.
No branch of agriculture in Canada can remain static. It either goes forward or retrogresses. Never in history has the need for co-operation been greater than at the present time. The task of producing good food economically and of placing it where the thousands of hungry people require it, is one of extreme magnitude. It is suggested that, in so far as land use is concerned, this is a responsibility of the federal and provincial governments. We must embark upon a vast program of economic classification of our land. We must examine the position of agricultural areas in relation to the use of natural resources, land settlement, land productivity, standards of living, opportunities for the uniting of farms and the chances given for employment in other work for those who wish to leave employment on the farms.
The spread between the farmer's cost and his revenue from the sale of his products is serious. In my opinion, land use plays an extremely important role in this connection. The feeding of the poor of the world is not an agricultural problem, in my opinion, and
Marginal Lands
cannot be pinned to the farmer. It is a social issue and can only be treated as such. Personally, I do not feel that the control of production is a serious matter but in some fields this tool should be used. The exception to this statement at the present moment is in regard to wheat and butter. I have made a few inquiries today in connection with butter and I should like to give you some figures in this regard. These figures were supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Butter production per capita in Canada in
1957	was 20.3 pounds, in 1958 it was 19.1 pounds and in 1959 it was 18.1 pounds. From these figures you will notice that there is a gradual decline in the per capita consumption of butter. How do the figures in regard to margarine compare? In 1957 the consumption of margarine per capita was 7.8 pounds, in
1958	it was 8.5 pounds and in 1959 it was 8.7 pounds. You will notice in this case a gradual increase in the consumption.
I have some figures taken from pages 112 to 114 of the Statistical Review of 1959 showing the production of creamery butter and margarine in Canada. These figures run from 23.32 million pounds per year to 28.01 million pounds per year. Incidentally, these figures are for the years 1949 to 1958. The highest production was in 1958, being 28.01 million pounds.
In 1949 the production of margarine was 6.16 million pounds and it has gradually increased over the years until at the end of 1958 we find 12.13 million pounds produced.
I believe that one of the things hurting butter consumption today is fear of heart disease. This fear has been created throughout the country by press reports and in other ways, and even though I am sitting beside a medical adviser I am not convinced that the consumption of butter will do much damage to my heart, at least.
I have just received some figures from the dominion bureau of statistics but I have not had much time to look them over. These figures concern the number of deaths from heart disease in Canada from 1950 to 1959 and show a gradual increase to 48,244. I will give the figures for the years 1950 to 1959. In 1950 the number of deaths from heart disease in Canada was 38,000; in 1951, 39,000; in 1952, 40,000; in 1953, 41,000; in 1954, 41,000; in 1955, 42,000; in 1956, 43,000; in 1957, 45,000; in 1958, 46,000; and in 1959, 48,000.
I admit, of course, that the population of Canada has increased during the same years, a fact which accounts in some degree for the increased number of deaths in Canada per year. Let us look at the percentage of deaths from heart disease during this same period of time. In 1950 the percentage was 31.3; in

Marginal Lands
1951, 31.3; in 1952, 32.2; in 1953, 32.4; then in 1954, it rose to 32.2 per cent; in 1955, 33.5; in 1956, 33.3; in 1957, 32.4; in 1958, 34.0; and in 1959, 34.5.
Let us at this stage consider this situation. It we believe that the consumption of butter in Canada caused this increase in the number of deaths from heart disease, how can we explain the fact that the consumption of butter has been declining? Perhaps the increase in deaths has arisen as a result of the increase in the consumption of margarine in the last ten years.
Agricultural research no doubt increases production in Canada. We have an excellent supply of tools, equipment and personnel with which to do valuable research work in agriculture but surely no one within the sound of my voice would suggest that research in agriculture be curtailed as a method of controlling production. Research efficiency cannot be built up in a short time. This must take considerable time. I believe farmers' inefficiency is a major problem in our agricultural world today, and the resolution before us hits at the heart of this problem. I do not mean to suggest for one moment that we have a group of inefficient farmers in Canada. My suggestion is far from that. Many farmers are situated on poor land and cannot derive a desirable standard of living under these conditions. It has often been said that the public generally should support the unbalance in farming. This statement may be true over a short period of time but as a permanent policy it would be quite wrong. Things are moving fast in these days. The world today is a product of what we believed yesterday, and the world of tomorrow will be a product of what we believe now. If we are to avoid the mistakes of the past we must be prepared to accept our responsibilities in changing agriculture conditions.
There exists in the United States an agency known as the farmers home administration under the supervision of the United States department of agriculture and it provides almost the same assistance to the eligible farmers as the Veterans' Land Act provides. In other words, it provides farm operators with credit and technical assistance. Loans are made only when farmers are unable to obtain suitable credit at reasonable rates of interest from regular sources. This help is particularly suitable to small farms and provides farmers with assistance somewhat similar to that which the V.L.A. has provided in the past.
The Veterans' Land Act includes many features which, on analysis of the small farm problem, I suggest could be given consideration under this present program. Credit is

made available at moderate rates and payments are flexible. Title of the land is held by the department and the farm operator is provided with technical supervision. I feel that what we should envisage is a broad program of rural development.
I should like to quote from a report of the third annual workshop of the Canadian Agriculture Economic Society, 1958 on the small farm problem. This reads as follows:
To implement this program we will need many well qualified supervisors and managers. Happily in the farm finance field we already have a fine organization and developmental nucleus in the competent personnel of the Veterans' Land Act administration. We can build up the necessary resources and we already have the desire to work. What remains to be done and has to be started without any further delay is to speed up an active program.
I see no reason why similar arrangements cannot be made in eastern Canada, which I consider to be that part east of the great lakes. I would suggest that this arrangement could be similar in many respects to the community pasture program under the P.F.R.A. on the prairies.
Let me give you some figures from the 195859 P.F.R.A. reports. Since the inception of this program in 1937, 1,815,265 acres of land have been developed for pasture use. Sixty two pasture projects were in operation in 1958. They handled the equivalent of 117,032 head of cattle. The stock was owned by 5,835 patrons. I claim that this is big business.
A statement by Drummond and McKenzie relating to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, of January 1957 points out the drop in the labour force in agriculture. From 1946 to 1955 those engaged in agriculture represented only 30 per cent of the 1946 force. This fact is perhaps due to better wages in industry and the greater use of machinery which allowed lower production costs on farms.
Not likely more than 5 million acres of land can be released for other farm production because of the replacement of the horse by the tractor which has taken place. This figure could increase by a couple more million in 20 years as a result of the same trend.
If a community pasture program takes place in eastern Canada, it will of necessity take place slowly and gradually. It can make better use of marginal lands and will require certain supervision with supervisors having the power to control.
The moving of farm families is a problem where the farm has been held by a family for generations. If farms are to be taken over by the government in order to organize a community pasture the cost of some of the

land will be above its actual value because the owner is selling, in effect, more than the land.
The Gordon royal commission forecasts a population in Canada by 1980 of 26.7 million, or 70 per cent more than the population of 1955. The commission also made the following forecast with respect to the total consumption of major food items, taking 1951-55 as equalling 100 per cent: red meats will increase by 1980 to 214 per cent, an increase of 114 per cent; poultry will increase by 1980 to 218 per cent, an increase of 118 per cent; eggs will increase by 1980 to 231 per cent, an increase of 131 per cent; dairy products will increase by 1980 to 168 per cent, an increase of 68 per cent.
The total amount of grain consumed by livestock in 1954-55 was about 12 million tons. By 1980 it is estimated that there will be a 90 per cent increase in the consumption of grain by livestock.
If a program of tree planting is to take place it should not be delayed. Trees take time to mature for harvest; and I am of the opinion that if a program is to be inaugurated it must take place while there are in the north trees which may be utilized while the new trees are growing.
To sum up, I support this resolution in principle. I am proud to think that this government is providing courageous leadership in developing a land use program which should have the twofold effect of (a) creating increased export markets while (b) adjusting the unbalanced situation in respect to agricultural production. We must all realize, of course, that this program cannot be implemented in a decade but must be carefully planned so that it may be brought to its full development over a period of many, many years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words with respect to this resolution. As all hon. members are aware, Canada is a country richly endowed with natural resources and with a relatively small population. Canada has a population of approximately 18 million and a total land area of nearly 4 million square miles. Only 1 per cent of this land area is now in farms and one half of that 1 per cent is under cultivation. Actually, not too much of Canada's land surface is under cultivation, yet we must develop our resources to benefit all Canadians. This resolution will bring about a greater intensification of the use of our resources and perhaps also a greater diversification of agriculture generally in Canada.
This resolution proposes to take marginal land out of production and perhaps redirect existing production into the production of
Marginal Lands
other products. The year 1960 was a reasonably good one for agriculture on the prairie provinces with the exception of some local conditions. Some parts of my own constituency suffered from dry weather while other parts enjoyed good weather and achieved record crops. Field crops were good in all the western provinces and wheat production amounted to 490 million bushels with a slight increase in the acreage seeded. Under this resolution it is proposed to redirect acreage, so we must examine what products are grown and consider which can best be redirected.
Wheat production in 1960 was up 19 per cent over that of last year. The acreage was up only 1 per cent while the yield was up 18 per cent, in terms of the number of bushels produced. The yield accounted for most of the increase in production. I point this situation out merely to make it clear that any small amount of land taken out of wheat production will not be enough because the yield makes a big difference in the production and unless the acreage can be reduced by at least 10 per cent no great change in production will come about.
The yield of a particular product is what determines the amount that will be available to place on the market. As I said, in redirecting land out of wheat production I would think we must redirect at least 10 per cent of the land now used for the production of wheat. Approximately 21 million acres are now given over to the production of wheat so there would have to be the redirection of approximately 2 million acres in order to have a substantial effect on production.
In looking over the figures it will be seen that acreage has already been reduced in Alberta by nearly two and a half million acres. Ten years ago Alberta had a wheat acreage of something over 6 million acres. Today it is slightly over 4 million. A reduction of 2 million acres has already occurred in that province with respect to wheat production. This land has been redirected in the production of barley, oats and other more diversified forms of agriculture.
To redirect more land would take a tremendous effort and whether it will be accomplished through this resolution is something that only time will tell. It appears that we must maintain our export position in world wheat trade. Of course, like other hon. members of this house, I am thankful that we have boosted our wheat exports this year through what perhaps might be described as unexpected exports to communist countries.
While our exports to Great Britain and Germany were down in 1959 I hope that the wheat board, now that it comes under the minister's department, will concentrate on regaining the lost sales to those countries and

Marginal Lands
make every effort to maintain our exports in what we consider to be our regular markets and channels.
In looking at some other field crops it will be seen that barley acreage has increased in Alberta but domestic use has increased as well. Our exports of barley last year were 64 million bushels. Approximately 170 million bushels of barley were consumed at home with a carryover of 120 million bushels. We had a total production of about 230 million bushels. The carryover of which I spoke was at the end of the 1959-60 crop year. That carryover would not be described as a surplus. While I do not think there is too much room for a greater acreage seeded to barley, certainly the present acreage could be maintained without creating any undue burden in terms of storage problems.
The same story is applicable with respect to oats. Domestic consumption is up and while we have some oats in storage, they are not surplus amounts.
In examining our imports of agricultural products I could not help but notice that 12 million bushels of corn were imported last year. Corn is grown principally in Ontario and Manitoba. Acreage in Ontario has doubled in the past ten years and nearly 500,000 acres in Ontario were seeded to corn last year. Perhaps this acreage could be increased again in order to produce more corn and cut down our imports of this particular product which surely can be grown in Ontario and Manitoba and, certainly in the irrigated parts of Alberta. Last year we had an exceptionally good year for durum wheat, and a great deal of it was grown. In fact there was an open quota on durum wheat and no doubt we shall see greater acreages next year though production cannot be expanded to any great extent.
Actually, the oilseeds present the greatest hope for expansion, and this resolution could help by speeding up measures of irrigation which would allow for increased production. Production of flax has remained reasonably constant. There was a rise in exports last year and, no doubt, there will be an increase in the acreage set to flax seed this year. Rapeseed is becoming a prominent crop in western Canada, and I think a greater acreage could be put to rapeseed as a result of measures which could perhaps be adopted in consequence of the present motion, namely, greater land use, an intensification of irrigation efforts, and so on. In fact, production of rapeseed was up by 40 per cent last year and, generally speaking, the farmers did well growing this crop in western Canada. Although the average yield declined somewhat compared with previous years I think that

if the government were to take certain steps the acreage under this crop could be increased.
One of those steps would be to specify that rapeseed was a grain, thus allowing it to qualify for shipment at the same rates as those at which other grains are shipped through Canada. This step would reduce the cost of producing this product by something like two cents a pound and would greatly enhance the possibility of its taking over some of the acreage presently set to wheat. Another interesting thing about rapeseed is that only about 5 per cent of the margarine used in Canada contains rapeseed oil. I think that if we could develop domestic markets and lower the freight rate on rapeseed, in addition to creating land more suitable for the raising of this crop, rapeseed could play a more dominant part in our economy, particularly in western Canada. The same comments apply generally to sunflower seed and mustard seed. Production of these two crops could be developed and, perhaps, will be developed to a greater extent now that the new crushing plant has been opened in Lethbridge.
Most of the thought in western Canada in connection with this measure is directed to greater cattle production. Yet our marketings were 11 per cent higher in 1960 than they were in 1959 and our exports of cattle were down by something like 34 per cent. I point this out only to emphasize that while there may be room for a continued expansion of cattle herds in proportion to the expansion of our population, I cannot see the likelihood of their being increased to a point much ahead of the expansion of our population without prices being affected. Though prices remain steady, and even finished on an optimistic note at the end of 1960, I feel there is not much room for greatly increased numbers of cattle. Perhaps our consumption of meat could increase. I think it would increase if some of the chain stores did not feel they had to make such a large profit as they are now making, particularly on beef and pork.
Hog marketings were down last year by 20 per cent from the year before, and if conditions do not change overmuch, prices should remain reasonably steady. However, I do not think there is much room for any great expansion here.
To sum up with regard to the major products of western Canada, wheat is the only product in surplus as to which we should not like to see any increase in acreage. As for rapeseed, durum wheat, sunflower seed, mustard seed and, possibly flax, besides other vegetable crops including potatoes, these products lend themselves well to intensive

agriculture, the use of irrigation and so on, and there may possibly be increases in production.
I do not think the production of butter should be reduced. On the other hand, I think consumption should be increased. It is interesting to note that in Great Britain when they decreased the price of butter they found they immediately had more consumers of butter. They found that after they had decreased the price for a year, when they increased it a little the consumer continued to eat butter. But, first, the price had to be decreased in order to attract consumers away from margarine. So I would suggest we should maintain the small dairy herd. A great many farmers today still buy the food for their tables out of the weekly cream cheque and I do not think we should take any steps that would be likely to reduce this cheque; rather, I think we should increase the consumption of this product.
